Kāḷahastī
(‘[spider], serpent and elephant’)
------------------------------------------
Kāḷahastī is a well-known place of पिल्ग्रिमगे situated in the Chittor district of Andhra Pradesh. It is 27 kms. (16.5 miles) to the north-east of तिरुपति, one of the foremost places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in India. It lies between two hills—Śrīpuram and Mummiḍicoḷapuram—which form part of the seven hills surrounding तिरुपति. The river Suvarṇamukhi flows on one side of the town.
Kāḷahastīśvara TempleKāḷahastī is famous for its temple of शिव, known as Kāḷahastīśvara. This शिवलिङ्ग is one of the five elemental liṅgas (pañcabhūtaliṅgas) and is called Vāyuliṅga (liṅga associated with वायु or air). There is a lamp in the inner sanctum that is constantly flickering as if to prove this point, despite the lack of movement of air inside.
The entrance to the temple is from the south whereas the deity faces west. The main लिङ्ग is said to be svayambhū or self manifested. It is white in colour and has the shape of the trunk of an elephant with tusks on either side. It is untouched by human hands, even by the priest. अभिषेक (bathing) is done by pouring a mixture of water, milk, camphor and pañcāmṛta (See PAÑCĀMṚTA.). पूजा or worship is offered to the उत्सवमूर्ति or processional image.
It is interesting to note that neatly dressed Śaivaite ब्राह्मणस् conduct the worship which includes that of various images of deities kept inside.
The temple structure is very impress-ive. The gopuram (main tower) is 36.5 metres (120 feet) high. The entire temple seems to have been carved out of the side of a huge stone hill.
There is an underground shrine (9 metres or 30 ft. below the ground level) of गणेश, called पाताल-विनायक.
Many royal dynasties have contributed to the construction of the temple complex. The पल्लवस्, the Coḷas and the rulers of Vijayanagara are more prominent among them.
It should be mentioned here that the famous hundred-pillared hall of the temple was built by Kṛṣṇadevarāya (A.

.
It is believed that this Kāḷahastīśvara लिङ्ग is the same as that which was worshipped by the hunter-saint कण्णप्प, now considered as one of the 63 Nāyan-mārs (or नायनार्स्) (See NĀYANĀRS.), the well-known saints of the Tamil country.
According to the स्थलपुराण (local म्य्थोलोग्य्) this लिङ्ग had been worshipped by ब्रह्मा himself and a galaxy of the ancient ṛṣis in all the four युगस् (See YUGAS.). अर्जुन is said to have visited it during his पिल्ग्रिमगे. In the historical period, Nakkīrar (celebrated Tamil poet who flourished in the 3rd century B. C.) as also the great Nāyanmārs—Sambandhar, अप्पर् (both lived in the 7th century A. D.), माणिक्कवाचगर् (9th century A. D.) and सुन्दरमूर्ति (8th century A. D.)—also visited this temple.
Pārvatī, the divine consort of Lord शिव is known here as Jñānaprasannāmbā, and has a separate shrine for her. She is considered as the sister of Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara.
The temple has quite a few rare icons like those of वल्लभ-गणपति, महालक्ष्मी-गणपति and Sahasra-liṅgeśvara.
The temple campus contains a few minor shrines dedicated to काशी-Viśvanātha, Annapūrṇa, सूर्यनारायण, Sadyogaṇapati and सुब्रह्मण्य.
Apart from the big hundred-pillared मण्डप, there are other smaller ones also like the Jalakoṭi-मण्डप and Palagar-मण्डप.
There are two sacred wells known as Sūryapuṣkariṇī and Candrapuṣkariṇī.
Two separate temples dedicated to Durgāmbā and Kaṇṇabeśvara are situated on the surrounding hills.
The total number of festivals celebrated during the year is 85. Out of these the Mahāśivarātri is the biggest festival celebrated for ten days.
The उत्सवमूर्ति (processional images) is taken out in a procession on the third day during the सङ्क्रान्ति festival.
There are twelve tīrthas or holy places with ponds (or rivulets) in the nearby Kailāsagiri hills. The water of one of the tīrthas—the सरस्वती-tīrtha—is believed to be endowed with the power to make the dumb speak if drunk!
